sections.text:
World action models (WAMs) built on pretrained video generation models adapt quickly to new robotic tasks, but they forget previously learned tasks under sequential fine-tuning.

Experience replay (ER) mitigates such forgetting by rehearsing data of previous tasks, yet this data is often unavailable in robotics, where a policy is deployed as weights only and its training data is not shared along with it. In this work, we ask whether a WAM can achieve data-free continual learning by regenerating its own past.

Our key observation is that a WAM can indeed autoregressively regenerate complete rollouts of previously learned tasks and replay them to mitigate forgetting. However, replaying such raw rollouts still lags far behind replaying real data, which we attribute to two issues.

First, the WAM is unable to recognize task completion and keeps generating purposeless motion after the task is done. Second, under open-loop generation, the generated actions gradually drift away from the generated observations.

To address both issues, we present rectified generative replay (R$^2$-WAM), which truncates generated rollouts at task completion with an agentic evaluator and filters out rollouts whose actions are physically inconsistent with the observations.

On the four LIBERO suites and five real-world tasks, R$^2$-WAM reduces forgetting by over 90% relative to sequential fine-tuning and nearly matches ER without accessing any data from previous tasks.

Our analysis further reveals that forgetting in WAMs concentrates in inverse dynamics modeling: a forgotten WAM still produces visually plausible observations of previous tasks while its generated actions fail. Project page: https://kaipengfang.github.io/r2-wam/

summary.en: The paper addresses forgetting in world action models during sequential fine-tuning and presents R²-WAM, a data-free generative replay method. It truncates generated rollouts at task completion using an evaluator and filters rollouts with actions inconsistent with observations. On four LIBERO suites and five real-world tasks, the authors report over 90% less forgetting than sequential fine-tuning and performance close to experience replay, without accessing previous-task data. Their analysis locates forgetting mainly in inverse dynamics: observations can remain visually plausible while generated actions fail.

Safely executing long-horizon multi-arm tasks online in complex dynamic environments remains challenging. We propose a new distributed dynamic Gaussian belief propagation (DD-GBP) method that directly plans joint-space trajectories through parallel local inference.

A unified Gaussian-process (GP) parameterization connects adaptive planning horizons, interpolation-time factors, and continuous execution. Each robot maintains a local tree-structured factor graph and exchanges messages asynchronously over active inter-arm links.

Dynamic subnet reconstruction and event-triggered updates reduce communication and inference costs while responding to moving obstacles. We also provide theoretical analyses of local inference accuracy, anytime early stopping, triggered-replanning consistency, and GP-consistent execution.

In 50 long-horizon, multi-target four-arm scenes with moving obstacles, DD-GBP achieves $92.5\%$ collision-free all-target completion and the highest success rate among six representative baselines.

Scenario ablations demonstrate long-horizon safety and robustness to communication impairment and extreme conditions; success remains $86.0\%$ under $90\%$ packet loss. Execution results further show substantially suppressed extreme velocity and acceleration peaks relative to Syn-GBP.

On one workstation, obstacle-free tests with 30 coexisting arms retain $99.87\%$ success and a $15.80$ ms mean warm solve, exceeding 60 Hz and outperforming the compared methods in scalability. Dual-arm transport experiments under dynamic interference demonstrate online response and practical deployability.

To the best of our knowledge, these results establish a new state of the art for online long-horizon multi-arm planning in dynamic scenes.

sections.text:
Dexterous manipulation poses a challenging high-dimensional optimization problem, as useful behaviors require coordinated motion across many hand joints. In reinforcement learning (RL) and sampling-based trajectory optimization, exploration commonly relies on independent robot joint perturbations, making coordinated behaviors difficult to discover.

Prior work reduces this search space for grasp learning using low-dimensional spaces of coordinated joint motions learned from human hand data, but this restricts the expressivity required for general manipulation. Some combine learned and joint-space actions to restore expressivity, but this increases dimensionality and introduces redundancy.

We study these effects across diverse manipulation settings, varying action dimensionality, exploration strategy, and the source of human data. Our experiments suggest that human-motion priors are most effective when used to structure exploration rather than change the action representation.

Motivated by this finding, we propose EigenDEXplore, which induces correlated exploration by adding perturbations along human-derived eigenvectors to independent joint-space noise, leaving the action space unchanged.

Across multiple dexterous hands, EigenDEXplore consistently outperforms joint-space and learned action-space baselines in grasping, in-hand reorientation, and contact-rich manipulation.

These gains span unstructured and reference-guided RL, trajectory optimization, and sim-to-real deployment, and are largest in settings with less reward shaping and curriculum design.

summary.en: The paper studies exploration strategies for dexterous manipulation, varying action dimensionality, exploration method, and human-data source. Its experiments suggest human-motion priors are most effective when structuring exploration rather than changing the action representation. EigenDEXplore adds perturbations along human-derived eigenvectors to independent joint-space noise while leaving the action space unchanged. The authors report that it outperforms joint-space and learned action-space baselines across grasping, in-hand reorientation, and contact-rich manipulation. Evaluations span reinforcement learning, trajectory optimization, and sim-to-real deployment.
summary.zh: 论文研究灵巧操作中的探索方式，比较动作维度、探索策略及人类动作数据来源。作者的实验表明，人类运动先验更适合用于组织探索，而非改变动作表示。据此提出 EigenDEXplore：在独立关节空间噪声上加入沿人类动作导出特征向量的扰动，同时保持动作空间不变。作者报告该方法在多种灵巧手的抓取、手内重定向和接触丰富操作任务中优于关节空间及学习动作空间基线；实验涵盖强化学习、轨迹优化及仿真到现实部署。

items.title: EigenDEXplore: Structured Exploration for Dexterous Manipulation with Human Priors

sections.text:
Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents.

Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: （1） functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, （2） a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and （3） cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues.

We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths.

Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%.Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works.

Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.

summary.en: The paper examines goal misgeneralization across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, identifying functional target substitution, policy shortcuts, and competition between intended and proxy goal cues. It traces whether goal information remains internally available, influences the policy, and contributes to action selection. In cue competition, steering raises intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. In the action-shortcut environment, new downstream wiring raises reach from 31.6% to 84.3%. Neither recovery method works when the goal information is inert. The authors characterize these as distinct alignment failures.
summary.zh: 论文在三个 Procgen 环境和五项机器人任务中研究目标误泛化，并区分三类目标与策略失配：功能性目标替代、策略捷径，以及预期目标线索与代理线索竞争。作者通过追踪目标信息的内部可用性、对策略的影响及其在决策中的作用，分析目标在不同深度失效的情形。在线索竞争中，转向使目标到达率从 16.0% 升至 95.3%；动作捷径环境中，新增下游连接使其从 31.6% 升至 84.3%；目标信息不起作用时，两种恢复方法均无效。

items.title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions.

However, most existing VLA models still operate on image-level visual representations inherited from pretrained vision-language backbones, while lacking fine-grained object understanding for manipulation. As a result, their robustness can degrade under out-of-distribution object layouts, clutter, and background variations.

To address these limitations, we introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction.

ObjDream uses a spatio-temporal object encoder to organize visual observations into temporal object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels.

These structured object representations are inserted into the token sequence of the vision-language model (VLM), where identity-guided routing modulates VLM attention to the corresponding object tokens.

In addition, an action-conditioned object dynamics module predicts compact future object states relevant to manipulation during training, explicitly supervising object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference.

Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 show that ObjDream improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and scene perturbations. Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate that ObjDream transfers to physical manipulation settings with novel object arrangements and background changes.

items.title: ObjDream: Guiding Vision-Language-Action Models with Object-Level Understanding and Future State Prediction

Though modern AI models like LLMs predict discrete tokens, today's robotic foundation models represent actions as continuous vectors. In this paper, we challenge this common consensus by asking if continuous action parametrizations are superior to their discrete counterparts.

We conduct an extensive comparison of single-step regression and multi-step flow variants of both continuous and discrete policies in both from-scratch single-task and multi-task VLA training, in both simulation and on real hardware.

In all regimes, we find that discrete action prediction, even the most naive, uniform-bin quantization, can match or even outperform continuous-action policies in task success rate.

Moreover, we find that the challenge to discrete action policies is \emph{not} action precision, but rather factorization error introduced by product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions.

We show that, when paired with the correct interventions---iterative computation through discrete flows, or distribution sharpening through classifier-free guidance---discrete flow policies can turn this weakness into a strength, enabling more responsive action changes during a predicted action chunk.

Lastly, we show that attempts to explicitly inject geometric information into discrete policies, e.g. through corruption processes that emulate continuous flow matching, do \emph{not} yield consistent improvements.

Taken together, our findings question existing assumptions that robotic action prediction requires distinct design decisions compared to other AI domains, and motivates the possibility of discrete action prediction as a compelling alternative to today's continuous action parametrizations.

Efficiently tackling multiple tasks within complex environments, such as those found in robot manipulation, remains an ongoing challenge in robotics and an opportunity for data-driven solutions such as reinforcement learning (RL).

The high cost of data gathering in robotics encourages data-efficient approaches such as model-based RL, which builds a dynamic model of the robot to conduct most policy learning on cheaper simulations, while enabling data reuse and transfer between tasks. In this work, we employ Bayesian deep learning (BDL) with a double purpose.

First, we increase the model quality by improving its calibration. Second, we improve data efficiency by performing active learning of the dynamic model during a preliminary exploration phase, actively estimating the information gain of each transition and using it as the exploration reward.

We compare several BDL methods in a realistic robot manipulation setup.

Our experiments show that our approach matches the quality of relevant alternatives with much lower robot execution requirements and, unlike previous studies validated only on standard RL environments, we tackle robotic arm end-tasks on a complete manipulator simulator such as \texttt{CoppeliaSim}.

Code is available at https://github.com/ropertunizar/BayesianActiveExploration.

items.title: Active Exploration in Bayesian Model-based Reinforcement Learning for Robot Manipulation

When an off-the-shelf coding agent is used directly as a robot policy, observing a browser-based 3D interface through screenshots and acting by posing a virtual target gripper through a few tools, the agent's harness, its prompts, tools, and control rules, largely determines success, and until now it has been written by hand.

We show that this harness can be improved automatically by another coding agent, the optimizer agent, and report two findings about what makes it work.

First, the number of rollouts the optimizer agent sees per round governs whether the evolved harness generalizes: with rounds fixed, held-out success rises as the training batch grows from 5 to 100 rollouts, while small batches overfit the training tasks. Second, the optimizer agent must not be given free rein.

Accepting every revision it proposes degrades the harness within a few rounds; a simple Champion-Challenger rule that promotes a revision only if it beats the incumbent on the same fixed cases turns the same loop into one that raises held-out success on LIBERO tasks from 51% to 67% over 30 rounds.

Combining the evolved harness with a pretrained policy, through one tool that hands it control, reaches 71.2% on the RoboCasa365 leaderboard benchmark, 13.1 points above the best published entry.

Automatic harness evolution for visual-interface robot agents is thus feasible, but its gains hinge on the rollout scale behind each decision and on how the optimizer agent's revisions are selected.

items.title: Scale and Selection: What Makes Automatic Harness Evolution Work for Visual-Interface Robot Agents

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment.

We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals.

During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines.

Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.

items.title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning

This paper investigates the use of Behavior Cloning (BC) for autonomous driving from a bird's-eye view (BEV) perspective in simulated urban environments. BC uses supervised learning to mimic expert driving behaviors. Previous works have applied BC in the CARLA simulator but did not fully address the challenges of traffic light compliance.

Our approach enhances BC by integrating a kernel density estimator to adjust training sample weights based on action density, thereby improving the learning of rare but critical actions such as stopping at red lights and accelerating at green lights, specially in scenarios of scarce number of expert demonstrations.

Using BEV inputs, which provide an abstract top-down view of the driving environment, our method simplifies the policy learning process. The trained convolutional neural network (CNN) outputs steering and acceleration actions based on these BEV inputs and additional state variables.

Experimental results in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that our weighted BC method significantly improves driving performance, achieving higher route completion compared to standard BC.

This weighted approach proved to be crucial in learning correct driving behaviors, particularly in test environments not encountered during training, highlighting its potential for enhancing autonomous vehicle navigation.

items.title: Investigating Behavior Cloning from Few Demonstrations for Autonomous Driving based on Bird's-Eye View in Simulated Cities

Despite the Markov assumption, safety failures in robot reinforcement learning rarely occur instantaneously; they typically emerge over several steps as the policy enters unfamiliar states under disturbances and domain shift.

We address this limitation by learning a receding-horizon safety critic that predicts whether a state will remain non-terminating over the next receding horizon, enabling anticipatory detection of impending locomotion failures.

The critic is trained from rollout-derived horizon labels with a composite objective that combines horizon classification, control-barrier-function-inspired temporal consistency, and smoothness regularization, and we aggregate an ensemble of critics with a conservative Conditional Value at Risk estimate to account for uncertainty.

Building on the learned critic, we derive a closed-form, differentiable CBF-style safety filter that minimally modifies the policy action to improve predicted safety, and integrate it into PPO with an anticipation loss to reduce policy-filter mismatch during training.

In simulated quadruped locomotion, our method improves robustness under action noise, external perturbations, and terrain shifts, reducing catastrophic failures while maintaining competitive returns.

items.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Receding-Horizon Safety Critic and Differentiable Action Shields
